title: ST558 Project 1
text:
The American Community Survey’s Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) contains anonymous survey responses for individual people. Each row comes with a weight, PWGTP, that tells us how many people in the population it represents. In this project we’ll write functions to pull PUMS data from the Census API for 2021–2024 and clean it into a tibble. Then we’ll write custom summary() and plot() methods that account for those weights. Finally, we’ll apply these tools to look at how commute times in New York changed over this time span.


We are going to query the Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) Census API. Information about this is available here: Information about PUMS API

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Parsing Variable Values
First, we’ll start by loading our required libraries. We need httr and jsonlite for the API, tidyverse for tibbles and lubridate, and hms for time values.

library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)
library(hms)

Now, we can move on to downloading and parsing the JSON files with variable descriptions for the years 2021-2024.
We only want to parse certain variables, so we’ll specify them below. We need to write a function to GET() the URL, parse the JSON, and pull out a list of variables with their values. We’ll obtain one list for each year.

vars <- c("AGEP", "GASP", "GRPIP", "JWAP", "JWDP", "JWMNP", "PWGTP",
               "FER", "HHL", "SCH", "SCHL", "SEX", "REGION", "DIVISION")
# ST: 2021-2022
# STATE: 2023-2024

#API Key - Required, should find some way to encrypt this in future
key <- "4270e8325c6e236168e18ec3682a2a6cc27469c7"

# Function
get_var_dict <- function(year) {
  if (length(year) != 1 || !(year %in% 2021:2024)) {
    stop("Year must be a single value between 2021 and 2024")
  }
  
  url <- paste0("https://api.census.gov/data/", year, "/acs/acs1/pums/variables.json?key=", key)
  response <- GET(url)
  stop_for_status(response)
  parsed <- fromJSON(content(response, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"), # Can also use the `rawToChar()` approach here 
                             simplifyVector = FALSE)
  
  state_var <- if (year <= 2022) "ST" else "STATE"
  
  #For each variable, keep a named character vector and sort by numeric order. Non-numeric codes become NA
  lapply(parsed$variables[c(vars, state_var)], function(variable) {
    items <- unlist(variable$values$item)
    code_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(names(items)))
    items[order(code_num)]
  })
}

var_dicts <- lapply(2021:2024, get_var_dict)
names(var_dicts) <- 2021:2024

We can then save these lists as an .rds file in the repo under a data folder. Using dir.create() creates the folder from scratch, and rerunning it without warnings does nothing, allowing for more replicability.

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(var_dicts, "data/var_dicts.rds")

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Parsing API Data
Now, we’ll want to write a function to query the PUMS API and return a nicely formatted tibble. When we query the API with our usual process, the data should come out nicely. Let’s start with an example of this.

# Testing via a hard-coded query, using state NC
url <- paste0("https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs1/pums",
              "?get=SEX,PWGTP,AGEP&for=state:37",
              "&key=", key)
response <- GET(url)
parsed <- fromJSON(content(response, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
head(parsed)

     [,1]  [,2]    [,3]   [,4]   
[1,] "SEX" "PWGTP" "AGEP" "state"
[2,] "1"   "60"    "23"   "37"   
[3,] "1"   "49"    "21"   "37"   
[4,] "1"   "24"    "20"   "37"   
[5,] "2"   "54"    "79"   "37"   
[6,] "1"   "79"    "18"   "37"   


Next, we’ll write a helper function to take what is returned by GET() and turn it into a nice tibble

response_to_tibble <- function(response) {
  stop_for_status(response)
  parsed <- fromJSON(content(response, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
  colnames(parsed) <- parsed[1, ]
  as_tibble(parsed[-1, , drop = FALSE]) # drop = FALSE keeps matrix shape for the tibble
}
# Testing on response from above
pums_tbl <- response_to_tibble(response)
str(pums_tbl)

tibble [114,270 × 4] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ SEX  : chr [1:114270] "1" "1" "1" "2" ...
 $ PWGTP: chr [1:114270] "60" "49" "24" "54" ...
 $ AGEP : chr [1:114270] "23" "21" "20" "79" ...
 $ state: chr [1:114270] "37" "37" "37" "37" ...


Then, let’s make some more helper functions to help us with our next step. These will convert variables into numeric values, normalize time codes and return the midpoint, and handle categorical variables by making them factors.

# Strip leading zeros to help standard time codes: "01", "1", and "001" all match
normalize_code <- function(x) {
   sub("^0+(?=.)", "", x, perl = TRUE) }

# Convert to numbers; codes labeled "N/A" in the dictionary become NA
convert_numeric <- function(x, labels) {
  na_codes <- normalize_code(names(labels)[grepl("^N/A", labels)])
  x_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  x_num[normalize_code(x) %in% na_codes] <- NA
  x_num
}

# Time: midpoint of each interval as a time of day ("N/A" labels become NA)
convert_time <- function(x, labels) {
  clean <- gsub("\\.", "", labels)   # "a.m." -> "am"
  start <- parse_date_time(sub(" to .*", "", clean), "I:M p", quiet = TRUE)
  end   <- parse_date_time(sub(".* to ", "", clean), "I:M p", quiet = TRUE)
  midpoint <- as_hms(start + (end - start) / 2)
  midpoint[match(normalize_code(x), normalize_code(names(labels)))]
}

# Categorical: factor with dictionary-ordered levels and readable labels
make_factor <- function(x, labels) {
  factor(normalize_code(x), levels = normalize_code(names(labels)), labels = labels)
}

Now, using our helper functions, we’ll wrap this into Our main function, query_pums(). This function lets the user choose the survey year, numeric and categorical variables, and a geography. We check every input and return a clear error if something isn’t allowed. If no geography value is given, we default to North Carolina (or the South region / South Atlantic division), and “all” returns every value at that level. Puerto Rico is excluded, and PWGTP is always returned since we need it for weighting.

query_pums <- function(year = 2024,
                       num_vars = c("AGEP", "PWGTP"),
                       cat_vars = "SEX",
                       geo_level = "State",
                       geo_value = NULL,
                       api_key = key) {
  # Stop if invalid year
  if (length(year) != 1 || !(year %in% 2021:2024)) {
    stop("year must be a single value: 2021, 2022, 2023, or 2024")
  }
  # Numeric variable options
  num_options <- c("AGEP", "GASP", "GRPIP", "JWAP", "JWDP", "JWMNP")
  num_vars <- toupper(num_vars)
  bad_num <- setdiff(num_vars, c(num_options, "PWGTP"))
  if (length(bad_num) > 0) {
    stop("Invalid numeric variable(s): ", paste(bad_num, collapse = ", "), # Stop if invalid numeric variables requested
         ". Choose from: ", paste(num_options, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (!any(num_vars %in% num_options)) {
    stop("Must request at least one numeric variable (other than PWGTP)") 
  }
  num_vars <- union(num_vars, "PWGTP")  # PWGTP is always returned
  # Categorical variable options
  cat_options <- c("FER", "HHL", "SCH", "SCHL", "SEX")
  cat_vars <- toupper(cat_vars)
  if (length(cat_vars) == 0) {
    stop("At least one categorical variable must be requested")
  }
  bad_cat <- setdiff(cat_vars, cat_options)
  if (length(bad_cat) > 0) {
    stop("Invalid categorical variable(s): ", paste(bad_cat, collapse = ", "), 
         ". Choose from: ", paste(cat_options, collapse = ", "))
  }
  # Geography level specification
  if (length(geo_level) != 1 ||
      !(tolower(geo_level) %in% c("region", "division", "state"))) {
    stop("geo_level must be one of 'Region', 'Division', or 'State'") 
  }
  geo_level <- tolower(geo_level)

  # Geography value options
  var_dicts <- readRDS("data/var_dicts.rds")
  geo_var <- switch(geo_level,
                    region   = "REGION",
                    division = "DIVISION",
                    state    = if (year <= 2022) "ST" else "STATE")
  geo_labels  <- var_dicts[[as.character(year)]][[geo_var]]
  valid_codes <- names(geo_labels)[!grepl("Puerto Rico", geo_labels)]

  # Defaults if no value given (chosen): South region (3), South Atlantic division (5), North Carolina (37)
  if (is.null(geo_value)) {
    geo_value <- switch(geo_level, region = "3", division = "5", state = "37")
  }

  if (length(geo_value) == 1 && tolower(geo_value) == "all") {
    geo_codes <- "*"
  } else {
    # Match integers so 1, "1", and "01" all work
    match_idx <- match(suppressWarnings(as.integer(geo_value)),
                       as.integer(valid_codes))
    if (anyNA(match_idx)) {
      stop("Invalid ", geo_level, " value(s): ", 
           paste(geo_value[is.na(match_idx)], collapse = ", "))
    }
    geo_codes <- paste(valid_codes[match_idx], collapse = ",")
  }
  # Query API and return a census tibble
  response <- GET(
    paste0("https://api.census.gov/data/", year, "/acs/acs1/pums"),
    query = list(get   = paste(c(num_vars, cat_vars), collapse = ","),
                 `for` = paste0(geo_level, ":", geo_codes),
                 key   = api_key)
  )
  pums_tbl <- response_to_tibble(response)
  
  # Convert column types using this years dictionary
  dict <- var_dicts[[as.character(year)]]
  for (v in num_vars) {
    pums_tbl[[v]] <- if (v %in% c("JWAP", "JWDP")) {
      convert_time(pums_tbl[[v]], dict[[v]])
    } else {
      convert_numeric(pums_tbl[[v]], dict[[v]])
    }
  }
  for (v in cat_vars) {
    pums_tbl[[v]] <- make_factor(pums_tbl[[v]], dict[[v]])
  }
  # droplevels() removes geographies that weren't requested
  pums_tbl[[geo_level]] <- droplevels(make_factor(pums_tbl[[geo_level]], dict[[geo_var]]))

  class(pums_tbl) <- c("census", class(pums_tbl))
  pums_tbl
}  

Now lets test our function with default values:

10    67    37 Female North Carolina/NC

# Specified values
nc_2022_test <- query_pums(2022,
                        num_vars = c("AGEP", "JWAP", "JWMNP"),
                        cat_vars = c("SEX", "SCHL"))
str(nc_2022_test)

The numeric variables are now real numbers, JWAP is stored as a time of day (NA for people without a commute), and SEX and SCHL are factors with readable labels instead of codes.

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Combining Years
Finally, lets write a function that allows the user to specify multiple years of survey data (along with all the other options). This function will call a single year function as many times as needed and then combine the data into one final tibble with a year variable included.

query_pums_combined <- function(years = 2024, ...) { # ... passes everything else to query_pums (not repeated)
  years <- sort(unique(years))
  if (length(years) == 0 || !all(years %in% 2021:2024)) {
    stop("Years must be one or more of: 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024")
  }

  # Query each year, add a year column, and drop the census class before binding
  results <- lapply(years, function(yr) {
    year_tbl <- query_pums(year = yr, ...)
    year_tbl$year <- yr
    class(year_tbl) <- setdiff(class(year_tbl), "census")
    year_tbl
  })

  combined <- bind_rows(results)
  combined$year <- factor(combined$year)

  class(combined) <- c("census", class(combined))
  combined
}

Testing a combined years query

multi <- query_pums_combined(c(2022, 2024),
                    num_vars = c("AGEP", "JWMNP"),
                    cat_vars = "SEX")
str(multi)

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Numeric Summaries
For the census summary method, we’ll write a function that produces means and standard deviations for our numeric variable(s) and counts for our categorical variable(s).

The function will take three arguments: the census tibble (maybe having multiple years), the numeric variable(s) to summarize, and the categorical variable(s) to summarize.
By default, it will summarize all numeric variables (other than PWGTP) and all categorical variables in the tibble. However, the user will be able to specify the variables they’d like to summarize.
All values will be returned as a named list


summary.census <- function(object, num_vars = NULL, cat_vars = NULL, ...) {
  weight <- object$PWGTP

  # Defaults: all numeric variables (except PWGTP) and all factors
  if (is.null(num_vars)) {
    num_vars <- names(object)[sapply(object, is.numeric)]
    num_vars <- setdiff(num_vars, "PWGTP")
  }
  if (is.null(cat_vars)) {
    cat_vars <- names(object)[sapply(object, is.factor)]
  }

  # Validate user input
  missing_vars <- setdiff(c(num_vars, cat_vars), names(object))
  if (length(missing_vars) > 0) {
    stop("Variable(s) not in the data: ", paste(missing_vars, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (!all(sapply(object[num_vars], is.numeric))) {
    stop("num_vars must be numeric, non-time variables")
  }
  if (!all(sapply(object[cat_vars], is.factor))) {
    stop("cat_vars must be categorical (factor) variables")
  }

  # Weighted mean and SD for each numeric variable, dropping NAs
  num_summaries <- lapply(num_vars, function(v) {
    keep <- !is.na(object[[v]])
    x <- object[[v]][keep]
    w <- weight[keep]
    mean_x <- sum(x * w) / sum(w)
    sd_x <- sqrt(sum(x^2 * w) / sum(w) - mean_x^2)
    c(mean = mean_x, sd = sd_x)
  })
  names(num_summaries) <- num_vars

  # Weighted counts for each categorical variable
  cat_summaries <- lapply(cat_vars, function(v) {
    tapply(weight, object[[v]], sum, default = 0)
  })
  names(cat_summaries) <- cat_vars

  list(numeric = num_summaries, categorical = cat_summaries)
}

In this function we are using weighted statistics Since a row with PWGTP = 50 stands for 50 people. Copying each row 50 times would make huge tibbles. Instead, because our data has the census class, R will automatically send summary() and plot() to our own versions of those functions, which handle the weights for us.

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Graphical Summaries
Similar to this process, let’s create a generic plot() function for a census class tibble. This will require the user to specify one categorical variable (can include year) and one numeric variable for plotting. The plot should create a boxplot of the numeric variable at the levels of the categorical variable.
Quickly, let’s also define some of the labels for our variables so our plots are more readable

# Readable labels for plot titles and axes
var_labels <- c(
  AGEP     = "Age (years)",
  GASP     = "Monthly gas cost ($)",
  GRPIP    = "Gross rent as % of household income",
  JWAP     = "Time of arrival at work",
  JWDP     = "Time of departure for work",
  JWMNP    = "Travel time to work (minutes)",
  FER      = "Gave birth in past 12 months",
  HHL      = "Household language",
  SCH      = "School enrollment",
  SCHL     = "Educational attainment",
  SEX      = "Sex",
  year     = "Survey year",
  state    = "State",
  region   = "Region",
  division = "Division"
)

# Return the readable label if one exists, otherwise the variable name
get_label <- function(var) {
  if (var %in% names(var_labels)) var_labels[[var]] else var
}

Now, let’s build our generic plot function

plot.census <- function(x, cat_var, num_var, colors = NULL, ...) {
  # Both variables are required
  if (missing(cat_var) || missing(num_var)) {
    stop("You must specify one categorical (cat_var) and one numeric (num_var) variable")
  }
  if (length(cat_var) != 1 || length(num_var) != 1) {
    stop("cat_var and num_var must each be a single variable name")
  }

  # Validate the categorical variable
  if (!(cat_var %in% names(x)) || !is.factor(x[[cat_var]])) {
    stop(cat_var, " is not a categorical (factor) variable in the data")
  }

  # Validate the numeric variable (time values are allowed)
  if (!(num_var %in% names(x)) ||
      !(is.numeric(x[[num_var]]) || inherits(x[[num_var]], "hms"))) {
    stop(num_var, " is not a numeric variable in the data")
  }
  if (num_var == "PWGTP") {
    stop("PWGTP is the weight variable; choose a different numeric variable")
  }

  # Drop rows with missing values, drop unused factor levels
  plot_data <- x[!is.na(x[[num_var]]) & !is.na(x[[cat_var]]), ]
  plot_data[[cat_var]] <- droplevels(plot_data[[cat_var]])

  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = get(cat_var), y = get(num_var),
                             weight = PWGTP, fill = get(cat_var))) +
    geom_boxplot(...) +                                    # pass extra options through
    labs(x = get_label(cat_var),                           # readable labels
         y = get_label(num_var),
         title = paste(get_label(num_var), "by", get_label(cat_var))) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")                        # x-axis already labels the boxes

  # Apply user-chosen colors, one per level of the categorical variable
  if (!is.null(colors)) {
    n_levels <- nlevels(plot_data[[cat_var]])
    if (length(colors) < n_levels) {
      stop("Need at least ", n_levels, " colors for the levels of ", cat_var)
    }
    p <- p + scale_fill_manual(values = colors)
  }

  p
}

Now, let’s test our plot function in several ways

# One categorical variable: year and numeric variable age
plot(multi, cat_var = "year", num_var = "AGEP", colors = c("gold", "forestgreen"))








Here is a boxplot of age in years by survey years. We see very little change here which is expected as the survey years are only two years apart.

# Categorical variable sex and numeric variable commute time
plot(multi, cat_var = "SEX", num_var = "JWMNP", colors = c("skyblue", "magenta"))








Here is a plot of travel time to work (in minutes) by sex. Both box plots are centered around 25 minutes, with women having a slightly larger IQR for commute times. There are also some clear outliers for commuters over an hour and a few ‘super commuters’ over two hours.

# Plot of time of arrival and sex with outliers lightened
plot(nc_2022_test, cat_var = "SEX", num_var = "JWAP", outlier.alpha = 0.05) # default colors








It’s important to note that we don’t use multi here because we are dealing with time, so we used our test query from earlier for 2022 NC data.
These box plots of time of arrival by sex have much more variance due to many workers who work night shifts or atypical hours. The median of the data is still around 9AM, with females having a slightly later median arrival time, from this data.
Now, let’s try a multi-level example of age by educational attainment using the same 2022 NC Data. Here we flip the coordinates for better readability since there are so many levels of education.

plot(nc_2022_test, cat_var = "SCHL", num_var = "AGEP") +
  coord_flip()








Here we see a clear trend of education level and age, with the lowest levels being mostly young kids still in school. There are a lot of outliers for older people who never received a formal education beyond a few grade levels.
Finally, here are some error cases that shouldn’t work

plot(nc_test_2022, cat_var = "year")                                         # missing num_var

Error: object 'nc_test_2022' not found

plot(nc_test_2022, cat_var = "AGEP", num_var = "SEX")                        # variables swapped

Error: object 'nc_test_2022' not found

plot(nc_test_2022, cat_var = "SCHL", num_var = "AGEP", colors = c("blue", "red"))  # too few colors

Error: object 'nc_test_2022' not found

title: ST558 Project 1
text:
Conclusion
In this project we built functions to query the PUMS API, convert raw codes into numbers, times, and labeled factors, and combine multiple years of data. Our summary() and plot() methods use the survey weights so results describe the population rather than raw rows. Using them, we found that New York’s average commute rose about two minutes after 2021 and has held near 33 minutes since. New York commutes are also longer than those in North Carolina or Texas. These are descriptive comparisons only, but give us an idea on computing formal tests in the future.
